In Table 10, the Darcy configuration attaining weak residual 0.915 still has strong residual 47.1 times the clean reference, versus 16.4 for PBFM. Helmholtz strong residuals also remain around ten times the reference. These discrepancies require investigation through independent solver-based accuracy checks and sensitivity to the weak-test construction.

The comparisons do not cleanly establish the benefit of joint evolution. Appendix E.2 acknowledges that conflicting training data and target physics disadvantage PBFM, while the ECI comparison enforces only boundaries. Stronger physics-aware post-training comparators are needed. Capacity- and regularization-matched ablations would also help separate joint evolution from the additional approximately six million parameters and trajectory regularization.

Claims of distribution preservation need qualification. For example, Table 13’s Stokes joint configuration with weak residual 4.72 has state/parameter MMDs of 0.882/0.266, compared with 0.224/0.049 before adaptation. The method offers a trade-off, but does not consistently preserve the reference distribution while substantially reducing residuals.

Reproducibility and statistical reporting remain incomplete despite the extensive appendix. Inverse-predictor training settings and numerical test-function scale ranges are missing; uncertainty notation is not clearly defined; and independent training-run variability and a validation protocol for configuration selection are not reported. The manuscript references released configurations but provides no accessible repository link.

The natural-image extension supplies visual examples without quantitative reward, fidelity, or diversity results, or a simple recoloring-only baseline. It therefore provides limited evidence for the claimed cross-domain advantage.

strengths: Addresses an important setting: adapting pretrained scientific generators when physical parameters are unobserved and paired parameter–solution training data are unavailable.

Joint state–parameter evolution is a useful methodological idea. Local weak-form residuals are well motivated for noisy fields and discontinuous coefficients because they reduce derivative requirements.

Experiments cover four PDE families and several forms of misspecification. Concrete improvements include reducing elasticity boundary MSE from 6.98e-5 to 1.71e-6 and Helmholtz state MMD from approximately 0.18 to 0.06.

The appendix provides substantial architectural and experimental detail, hyperparameter sweeps, relevant Adjoint Matching ablations, and non-curated samples. The reported short fine-tuning time is practically attractive.
weaknesses: The regularized control objective is not derived consistently. Equation 2 assumes a state cost, but Section 3.3 defines that cost using the trainable fine-tuned velocity, making it explicitly control-dependent. The corresponding optimality condition generally requires a direct derivative of this cost with respect to the control, which Equation 4 omits. A derivation accounting for this dependence is needed before claiming that the algorithm optimizes the stated objective.

The theoretical guarantee does not cover the implemented sampler. Lemma 1 establishes a schedule property for the original interpolant, but does not establish the required properties for the surrogate joint parameter dynamics. Implementation further regularizes the endpoint singularities, and all evaluations use deterministic sampling despite stochastic training. No proof or stochastic-versus-deterministic comparison establishes the claimed tilted distribution for this procedure. Algorithm 1 also appears to subtract drifts evaluated at different states, whereas Equation 2 requires a pointwise drift difference.

Accurate parameter recovery and posterior inference are insufficiently demonstrated. Marginal MMD and qualitative guided samples do not establish correct state–parameter coupling, reconstruction accuracy, or posterior calibration. There is also an explicit identifiability issue: in the elasticity setup, multiplying Young’s modulus everywhere by a positive constant leaves the displacement solution unchanged under the prescribed Dirichlet conditions. The paper needs explicit identifiability assumptions or parameter priors, quantitative inverse-problem evaluations, and observation-consistency and uncertainty checks.

The results support residual–distribution trade-offs more strongly than the claims of physically valid samples with preserved distributions. In Table 10, the Darcy configuration achieving weak residual 0.915 still has strong residual 47.1 times the clean reference, compared with 16.4 for PBFM. In Table 13, the joint Stokes configuration with weak residual 4.72 has state MMD 0.882 versus 0.224 for the base model. Solver-based solution errors would help establish the physical significance of these improvements.

Comparisons do not adequately isolate the proposed contribution. Appendix E.2 acknowledges that PBFM is disadvantaged by conflicting training data and target physics; the ECI comparison enforces boundaries without enforcing the interior PDE. The Adjoint Matching ablations are useful, but matched-capacity and matched-regularization controls are missing, as are stronger post-training residual-optimization or physics-guidance comparisons under the same information constraints.

Reproducibility and statistical validation remain incomplete despite the lengthy appendix. The inverse predictor’s pretraining schedule and several test-function hyperparameters are unspecified, no code link is provided, and independent training-run variability is not reported. The meaning and scaling of the tabulated ± quantities are unclear. MMD bandwidths are selected from pooled generated/reference samples, so comparisons also need validation with a common kernel and a reference-versus-reference baseline.
